newsitem.title: INDIA: India militants threaten more "gruesome acts".
newsitem.headline: India militants threaten more "gruesome acts".

text.p: Tribal militants fighting for a homeland in northeastern India claimed responsibility on Friday for a bomb attack on a train this week which killed dozens of people, and threatened more "gruesome acts".

The Bodoland Liberation Tigers Force (BLTF) released a statement in Assam state's biggest city, Guwahati, saying the outfit attacked the train on Monday because the government had refused to take up its demand for a separate tribal state.

"The Tigers carried out the bomb blast as both the central and state governments failed to take up the issue of separate Bodoland state by the end of December 1996," the statement, attributed to BLTF spokesman Maina Daimari, said.
"This compelled the BLTF to resort to snap the link between (the) northeast and (the) rest of the country," it added.
Two remote-controlled bombs exploded on a train track about 200 km (125 miles) west of Guwahati on Monday evening, ripping through a crowded passenger train, killing at least 33 people.
Two other attacks this week, believed to have been carried out by Bodo militants, severed important rail and road links in the northeastern state.

The BLTF, one of several Bodo groups fighting for either a separate state inside of India or a new nation, threatened to carry out "the most gruesome acts in the near future" unless the government bowed to its demands for a separate state.
"Tigers would not be silent spectators if innocent people are harassed in the name of maintaining law and order," the statement said.
"Unless the government formulates a policy to create a separate state, the BLTF will be compelled to commit the most gruesome acts in the near future," it said.
The army launched a search operation on Tuesday to hunt down the insurgents who planted the bombs on the train track near Sensapani town.

On Thursday, officials in Assam said the state government had asked New Delhi to send 130 paramilitary companies, or about 26,000 men, almost doubling the force already in the state of Assam, officials said.
The Bodos account for about 800,000 of Assam's 25 million people. Over the past two decades, swarms of immigrants have been allowed to settle in their traditional tribal lands, angering the Bodos.
Illegal logging on a massive scale has devastated their environment and added to their grievances, which include a fundamental distrust of the Assamese ability to govern the state.
Bodo tribals, living in northwest Assam between the north bank of the Brahmaputra river and the foothills of the Himalayas, are fighting for a homeland that would split the state in two.
Since 1987, Bodos have been fighting immigrants, security forces and, at times, themselves. Police say some 5,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence.

The train attack was the biggest blow so far in a campaign that appears to have been stepped up since Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda came to Guwahati in October offering money but no hope of independence or autonomy.
